test(seam): compare paths in one canonical spelling

Three review findings, all valid.

The layering rules compared `path.relative` output against forward-slash
literals with `===`. That holds on POSIX and fails on every Windows host,
where `src\core\console.ts` never equals `src/core/console.ts` — so the gate
would report both sanctioned edges as simultaneously unsanctioned and stale,
accusing untouched code of exactly what it exists to catch. Four sites had
the exposure; `browser-safe.ts` next door computes the same paths but only
ever renders them, which is why this arrived with this branch.

Fixed at the representation rather than at the comparisons: `repoRelative`
in `test/coverage/extract.ts` is now the single crossing where an OS path
becomes the spelling the suite compares on. Normalizing at each comparison
would have left the fifth site to be forgotten.

Its test is pinned but honest — on a POSIX host the assertion holds with or
without the canonicalization, so it gates only on Windows and the comment
says so. Green on this CI is not evidence the normalization survived, and
recording that is better than implying a check stronger than the one there.

The transitive-cycle fixture carried a comment left over from an earlier
draft, naming rule.ts and console.ts while the fixture used color.ts and
panel.ts. Replaced with the chain it actually walks — panel.ts reaches
color.ts through core/style.ts — and shorter than the wrong version, since
the repair is to say the true thing once.

CLAUDE.md described the gate as failing two ways when it now fails three,
omitting the cycle check — which is the one that makes the safety claims in
the bullets directly above it verified rather than asserted. A reader
checking whether anything backs those claims would have concluded nothing
did.

test(seam): verify the sanctioned edges close no cycle

Three review findings, all valid.

Every `why` on a sanctioned edge argued the same safety property in its own
words — the edge points up, but it closes no module-level cycle — and
nothing re-read those words. A gate whose exemptions rest on unverified
claims is the exact shape this file was written to retire, so the fix is to
check the property rather than to stop advertising it.

`cyclicSanctionedEdges` asks it generically: for each sanctioned edge, the
runtime walk from the target must not reach the source. Deliberately a
*module* cycle rather than a layer one, because the two edges are safe for
different reasons and only this question covers both — `themes/palette.ts`
never returns to core at runtime, while `renderables/rule.ts` imports four
core primitives and is safe because none reaches `core/console.ts`. A
reciprocal "the import back must stay type-only" rule would have been wrong
about the second edge and right about the first by coincidence.

`isInside` was a second implementation of the four-part path-containment
idiom `isUnderSrc` already had, comment and all. Both now call one
`isPathInside`, so hardening it cannot leave one caller behind in the
string-prefix bug the layering test pins.

The CLAUDE.md sentence claiming the removed grep matched same-directory
imports only was false: the pattern actually removed was
`from "\.\.?/[a-z/]+\.js"`, which matches `../` and would have found both
edges. That was PR #66's pattern, corrected in this file long before this
branch, and the sentence is rewritten to attribute it and to give the real
argument for a gate over a working grep — a grep judges no sanction and
cannot see an exemption that outlived its import.

Both new rules falsified against real source: a runtime import added from
palette.ts back to color.ts turns the cycle gate red alone, and reinstating
the string-prefix bug in the shared helper turns the sibling-directory test
red.

test(seam): forbid upward imports out of core (rich-seam-981.5)

CLAUDE.md claimed `src/core/` has no upward calls and told the reader to
verify it with a grep. The grep in that section — `from "\./[a-z]+\.js"` —
matched same-directory imports only, so it could not have found either of
the two edges that actually leave core. A reader following the instruction
got a clean result from a check incapable of returning anything else.

`test/seam/layering.test.ts` replaces it: walk every file under `src/core/`,
resolve every import, fail naming file, line and specifier when an edge
leaves the layer without a sanction — and fail the other way too, when a
sanction outlives the import it permitted, so the exemption list cannot
accumulate permissions nobody needs.

The rule counts type-only imports, deliberately. `browser-safe.ts` skips
erased edges because a browser cannot trip over one; a layer can, because
`import type { Panel } from "../renderables/"` is core knowing the shape of
renderables. Rather than a flag selecting between two collectors, or a
second traversal making one fact into two maps, `moduleSpecifiers` now tags
each edge with `erased` and `runtimeModuleSpecifiers` derives by filtering.

The two sanctioned edges (`color.ts -> themes/palette.ts`,
`console.ts -> renderables/rule.ts`) are kept, as CLAUDE.md already records
them. `Console.rule()` stays — it is documented and tested — but the
duplicate `RuleOptions` that `console.ts` declared beside `rule.ts`'s is
gone, along with the field-by-field forwarding that existed only to bridge
the two copies.

Every rule was falsified against real source: a runtime upward import, a
type-only upward import, a removed sanctioned edge, and a blinded collector
each turn exactly the intended gate red.

test(seam): fail the unit suite when the barrel stops being browser-safe (rich-seam-981.4) (#73)

* test(seam): fail the unit suite when the barrel stops being browser-safe (rich-seam-981.4)

The browser-safe barrel was a claim in README.md and CLAUDE.md plus a grep
someone ran by hand and pasted into a ticket. The only automated guard was
indirect — vite bundles examples/, Playwright boots them in Chromium — which
catches a leak after a full docs build and a browser install, and reports it
as "a demo failed to boot" rather than naming the import.

test/seam/graph.ts walks the runtime import graph from a set of roots,
bounded to src/, carrying the chain that reached each module. It needs no
ts.Program: reachability is syntactic, and an `import type` edge is erased
before the module runs, so it is not an edge. A relative specifier that
fails to resolve throws rather than silently shrinking the graph.

test/seam/browser-safe.ts is the rule, pure over one parsed file: a `node:*`
specifier on an edge that survives to runtime, or a read of ambient
`process`/`Buffer` at module scope. Module scope is the line — color.ts and
console.ts both read `process` from inside a function body, where the read
happens only if a caller asks for it. There is no exemption for a module-scope
`typeof process` guard: nothing needs one, and the fix is always a function.

Roots come from package.json#exports minus src/node/, so a new subpath is
covered the moment it lands. loadCompilerOptions and isUnderSrc are now
exported from the coverage verifier rather than restated here.

Falsified both halves rather than trusting a green check. Adding
`import { readFileSync } from "node:fs"` to src/core/segment.ts fails with
`src/core/segment.ts:1 — imports "node:fs" / reached by: src/index.ts →
src/core/segment.ts`; adding `import "../node/save.js"` instead fails with
the three-hop chain through the airlock. The scanner's own shapes — type-only
imports, function bodies, class field initializers, name slots vs reads — are
pinned by fixtures.

CLAUDE.md's browser-safe section said the failure "does not land on the person
who wrote the import". That is no longer true, so it now says what does.

* test(seam): close the scanner's blind spots and false positives

Six holes, all found by review, four of them shapes the module's own
comment claimed it did not have.

A Node builtin imported without the `node:` prefix — `from "fs"` — type
checks here, resolves outside src/ so the walk skips it, and matched no
rule. `builtinModules` from the running Node now backs the check; it
already carries the slashed forms, so membership is one lookup.

Deferred execution was two half-truths. A function body was pruned even
when the function is immediately invoked, so `(() => process.env)()` at
module scope read nothing; parameter defaults were not pruned at all, so
`function ask(out = process.stdout) {}` reported a read that only happens
on a call. Both are the same question — does this wait for someone to call
the function — so they are now one predicate, which is what makes
`(function (o = process.stdout) {})()` come out right where two carve-outs
would each have missed the other's exception.

`ambient` meant *spelled* `process`, so a module declaring or importing its
own binding of that name failed a gate about Node globals. It now means
spelled `process` and bound nowhere in this module, collected from
`sf.statements` — no checker, no scope walk. A binding inside a
module-scope block still reports; that is the safe direction.

`const { process: local } = config` named a property of `config` and was
read as the global. `BindingElement.propertyName` is a name slot.

The `ShorthandPropertyAssignment` carve-out was the one branch in
`isNameSlot` written to make something fire and the one with no test that
it fires. It has one now.

CLAUDE.md's new paragraph restated this module's header nearly verbatim —
the two-descriptions-of-one-surface trap the file warns about thirty lines
earlier, added by the commit whose purpose was fixing an instance of it. It
is now the pointer it should have been, and shorter than what it replaced.

* test(seam): erasure, shadowing and heritage were each half a rule

Ten findings, and three of them were the round-1 fixes having bought their
own defects.

Erasure was read at the declaration only. `import { type Stats } from
"node:fs"` leaves `importClause.isTypeOnly` false — verified, not assumed —
so the per-specifier form `isolatedModules` encourages reported a specifier
that never survives. The question is now whether anything in the statement
survives: a default or namespace binding survives whatever the braces say,
a side-effect import has nothing to erase, and a named list erases only
when every element carries its own modifier.

Shadowing counted type-space declarations. `interface Buffer {}` shadows
the type and leaves the value where it was, so it suppressed a genuine
read — a false negative, bought by the fix for a false positive, in the
direction this file calls the worse one. Interfaces and type aliases are
out; so are type-only imports and specifiers, which bind nothing to shadow
with.

`ts.isTypeNode` calls a class `extends` clause a type node. It is an
expression that evaluates to the superclass the instant the declaration
runs, so the blanket prune hid `class Host extends Buffer {}` entirely. An
interface's `extends` produces the same node under the same token and *is*
erased, so the carve-out asks the heritage clause's parent as well.

An export specifier's local reference is `propertyName ?? name`, and it is
local only without a `from` clause — one rule, because the two spellings
pull opposite ways: `export { process }` reads the binding, `export
{ process } from "./m.js"` does not. Elsewhere a `propertyName` names a
slot in another table — an object's property, another module's export —
which covers the renamed import the same way.

A constructor is never the callee; its class is. `new (class {
constructor(o = process.stdout) {} })()` deferred a parameter default that
runs on load.

`global` joins the ambient list: Node-only, no browser counterpart, and
unlike the CommonJS names it has no backstop in an ESM package.

CLAUDE.md said "its header comment" of a paragraph naming only the test
file, while the rationale lives in the implementation file. Named it.

* test(seam): one deferral rule, three triggers

Three findings, and the useful one is that the deferral rule was right in
substance and applied to only one of the three places it belongs.

A function's body waits for a call. So does a constructor's — via its class.
An instance field waits for construction, and an accessor body waits for a
property read. All four are the same question, and the scan was answering it
for two of them: an instance field initializer was flagged even though
importing the module never runs it, which contradicted the constructor body
directly above it that the same file already deferred.

So `isDeferred` asks it once, and `isImmediatelyRun` picks the trigger.
`isImmediatelyRead` is `isImmediatelyInvoked` with the other syntax, sharing
the parenthesis walk. An accessor consults the read trigger because it has no
callable form — asking it the call question would always answer no, which is
what hid `{ get w() { return process.env } }.w`.

Static fields and `static {}` blocks wait for nothing; they run with the
declaration and are not pruned. The static block already worked, because
`ts.isFunctionLike` excludes it — now by fixture rather than by luck.

The header said the ambient rule fires on `process` or `Buffer` while
`AMBIENT_GLOBALS` held three names, stale from the commit that added the
third. It now names the constant, so the list has one home and the sentence
cannot disagree with it.

Two findings were declined on evidence rather than argument. `import {} from
"node:fs"` is not preserved by the emitter: compiled under this repo's
settings in an ESM package, it and `export {} from "node:os"` and
`import { type Stats }` all vanish, leaving only the unrelated export — so
treating an empty named clause as erased is what the emitter does. And
`export * as process from "./m.js"` binds nothing locally; tsc answers a
later `process.env` with "Cannot find name 'process'", having gone looking
for the global, so flagging it is correct and collecting the name would buy
back the false negative the interface finding just removed.

* test(seam): the trigger is one notion, not a branch per shape

Two findings asked for a branch each — a getter reached through
`new (…)().w`, a method through `(…).m()`. Taking them that way is an
enumeration with no cap, because consumption chains compose and the next
report would be `new (…)().m()`.

The closed version underneath is one notion: the container's value — the
object or class as written, or what `new` makes of it — is consumed right
here. Asked of the four function-like member kinds, which is an enumeration
that ends. A plain function is its own container and is consumed by a call;
a constructor's class by `new`; an accessor by a property read; a method by
that read being called. Neither an accessor nor a method has a callable form
of its own, so asking either the plain-call question could only ever answer
no — the same reason the getter case failed before.

Pruning a whole `PropertyDeclaration` hid its computed name, which runs when
the class body does whether or not the member is static. Only the initializer
is deferred now, which is both narrower and correct, and brings decorators
along for free. The parameter branch legitimately differs: a parameter name
can never be an expression, so pruning the whole parameter is safe there.

`export { type process }` referenced nothing at runtime and was read as a
live local reference — the import side of that question was already asked in
graph.ts.

`resolveEdge`'s throw is the walk's guard against silently narrowing the
graph, and nothing in a healthy `src/` had ever made it fire: the one line
whose regression would look exactly like success. It is exported and pinned,
with the null arm pinned beside it, rather than tested through a broken
fixture on disk that `tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` would reject.

Each new rule was falsified against its own fixture: neutering the method
trigger and the `new` unwrapping fails exactly the consumed-on-the-spot
test, restoring the coarse property prune fails exactly the class test, and
narrowing the throw fails exactly the resolve test.

* docs: leave the ambient-globals list one home

Last round I stopped `browser-safe.ts`'s header from enumerating
AMBIENT_GLOBALS, on the grounds that a list written twice is a list that
will disagree with itself — and in the same commit edited a sentence in
CLAUDE.md that was enumerating it, without noticing it was the same shape.
That sentence now names the constant too.

Fourth instance of one defect in this PR: prose beside code, made stale by
the commit that changed the code. The general form, which is what the next
sweep should look for: when prose enumerates something the code also
enumerates, point at the code's copy instead. Grepping for the changed
symbol never finds these — none of the four named one.
